source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO)
finding: A scaffold that forces an explicit ranked differential plus a devil's advocate and a test chooser beat the same base model prompted plainly, on accuracy and cost, in a hypothesis-then-test loop.
numbers: 304 NEJM CPC cases (2017-2025). Off-the-shelf o3 78.6% at $7,850/case. MAI-DxO (o3, no budget) 81.9% at $4,735. Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. Budgeted variant 79.9% at $2,396. 21 physicians (median 12 yrs): 19.9% at $2,963, 11.8 min, 6.6 questions, 7.2 tests.
limits: Hard cases chosen for difficulty; physicians barred from search and had no team; gatekeeper is an LLM that can invent test results; developed on GPT-4.1 with a train/validation/test split (test = 56 cases). Authors are Microsoft.
agent_relevance: S3 generate and S4 test work as a program-held loop: top-3 differential updated each round, tests picked to discriminate between hypotheses. Supports keeping a small explicit hypothesis list.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO): gains across models
finding: The orchestrator improved every sufficiently capable model tested; gains were largest for weaker baselines and small for o3/o4-mini, where cost fell instead.
numbers: Average gain about 11 percentage points across OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Llama families. One-sided paired permutation test, 10000 resamples: significant (p<0.005) for all models except o3 and o4-mini (accuracy), which had significant cost cuts (p<0.005).
limits: Model-by-model numbers are in a figure; the strongest base models gain least, so the scaffold may matter less as models improve.
agent_relevance: Benefit of the hypothesis-test scaffold shrinks with base-model strength. G7 (must pay for itself at equal tokens) applies; here token cost was negligible ($0.15 per case inference).

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO): failure modes seen in baseline
finding: Authors report by manual inspection that plain o3 anchored on initial impressions and ordered tests that were reasonable for the current differential rather than maximally informative; the scaffold sought disconfirming evidence and switched paths.
numbers: Case example: hand sanitizer ingestion. Plain o3 fixated on antibiotic toxicity, ordered brain MRI and EEG, wrong, $3,431. Scaffold asked about toxin exposure in round 1, correct, $795.
limits: Anecdotal case inspection, not a measured rate. No ablation of individual roles (hypothesis tracker vs challenger) reported in the main text.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G1-style doubt triggered by structure: an explicit falsification role. Cannot say which role carries the gain.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO): weak models and differential breadth
finding: Weaker models showed a false economy: they considered fewer differential diagnoses, so never ordered tests to confirm or exclude rivals. Accuracy correlated with cost for reasoning models.
numbers: Off-the-shelf Pareto frontier: 30-50% accuracy at low spend, 70-79% at $4,000-7,900.
limits: Interpretation by authors, not tested with a controlled manipulation of differential size.
agent_relevance: Number of hypotheses held may still matter for LLMs even though human experts did not generate more, only better ones. Test directly: cap vs widen S3 breadth.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompting an LLM to imitate clinical reasoning styles (including differential diagnosis formation, the hypothetico-deductive step) did not raise accuracy over plain chain of thought; for GPT-3.5 it lowered it.
numbers: MedQA USMLE step 2/3 diagnosis items, 95 for prompt development, 518 test. GPT-3.5: CoT 46%; intuitive 48% (P=0.9); analytic 40% (-6 pts, P=0.001); differential diagnosis 38% (-8 pts, P<0.001); Bayesian 42% (-4 pts, P=0.02).
limits: Multiple-choice vignettes where all data are given at once, so no data-search stage; two worked examples per prompt; single dataset.
agent_relevance: Writing out a differential in text is not a gain by itself for a weak model. Gain in MAI-DxO comes from the loop with new data, not from the list alone.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine: GPT-4
finding: With GPT-4 the same reasoning-style prompts were roughly neutral on accuracy while giving readable, clinician-like rationales.
numbers: GPT-4: CoT 76%; intuitive 77% (+0.8, P=0.73); differential diagnosis 78% (+2.2, CI -1.4 to +5.8, P=0.24); analytic 78% (+1.6, P=0.35); Bayesian 72% (-3.4, CI -7.0 to +0.3, P=0.07). Kappa 0.99 inter-rater.
limits: Not significant; the study was not powered for small gains. Rationale faithfulness not verified.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-style prompt is an interpretability tool at no accuracy cost for a strong model. Do not count on it for accuracy.

source: McDuff et al. (2023/2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: An LLM tuned for differential diagnosis beat unassisted clinicians at listing the right diagnosis, and helped clinicians when used as an aid, more than search did.
numbers: 302 NEJM cases, 20 clinicians, two read each case. Top-10 accuracy: LLM alone 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6% (p=0.04). Assisted: LLM 51.7% vs search 44.4% (p=0.03) vs unassisted 36.1% (McNemar 45.7, p<0.01).
limits: Whole case given up front (no sequential search); top-10 list scoring rewards breadth; clinicians barred from specialist consults; Google authors.
agent_relevance: Breadth of the differential is where LLM help shows. A cheap first step S3 that widens the list may help most when the final choice is made after tests.

source: McDuff et al. (2023/2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models: first-pass vs assisted
finding: Clinicians given the LLM produced more comprehensive differential lists than those without it.
numbers: Each clinician wrote an unassisted differential first, then an assisted one (stage 1 and stage 2 design).
limits: Order effect: the second differential always comes after the first, so some gain may come from simply thinking twice. Authors compared against a search arm, which controls part of this.
agent_relevance: Two-pass generation (unassisted then assisted) is a design pattern; second pass gain is confounded with reflection.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Giving physicians access to GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning score, though the LLM alone scored higher than physicians.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 60 min, up to 6 vignettes. Median score per case 76% (IQR 66-87) with LLM vs 74% (IQR 63-84) without; adjusted difference 2 pts (95% CI -4 to 8). Time per case 519 s vs 565 s (diff -82 s, CI -195 to 31). LLM alone 92% median over 3 runs; 16 pts above control (CI 2 to 30).
limits: Single month of data, mostly junior physicians, little prompt training, scoring covers differential, supporting and opposing findings, next steps. Human+LLM did worse than LLM alone.
agent_relevance: Agents should not be assumed to profit from a human-style partner. For our single agent: the strongest setting may be the agent doing S3/S4 itself under code control.

source: Bass et al. (2013) Experienced physicians benefit from analyzing initial diagnostic hypotheses
finding: Asking physicians to analyse their initial hypothesis (hypothetico-deductive or scheme-inductive) before finalising raised accuracy sharply, including in experienced nephrologists.
numbers: 9 nephrologists and 6 nephrology residents, 10 cases each. Nephrologists: initial 31.1% to final 65.6% (p<0.001). Residents: 40.0% to 70.0% (p<0.001). Strategy by experience interaction p=0.02: residents OR 5.69 (95% CI 1.59-20.33) for scheme-inductive; nephrologists OR 0.57 (0.23-1.39), no strategy difference.
limits: Very small N; initial vs final is within-person so more case data between steps also helps; no control without the priming step; the odds ratio and p-value in the abstract disagree (p=0.07 printed).
agent_relevance: Support for a forced state-hypothesis-then-analyse-it-against-remaining-data step (S3 to S4). Strategy type mattered little for experts.

source: Coderre et al. (2003) Diagnostic reasoning strategies and diagnostic success
finding: In think-aloud gastroenterology cases, pure hypothetico-deductive reasoning had lower odds of success than pattern recognition or scheme-inductive reasoning.
numbers: Logistic regression across experts and non-experts and four presentations; odds of success significantly greater for pattern recognition and scheme-inductive than hypothetico-deductive (exact odds ratios not read: abstract only). Expertise and case content were independent predictors.
limits: Abstract only. Strategy was coded from talk, so it may follow success instead of cause it (easy cases invite pattern recognition).
agent_relevance: The classic hypothesis-driven method is not the best-performing human strategy. Do not make it the only route in the schema.

source: Ark, Brooks, Eva (2007) The benefits of flexibility
finding: Teaching novices to combine feature-by-feature analysis with trust in familiarity beat either alone, and contrastive learning helped too, with no interaction.
numbers: 48 naive students learning ECG diagnosis. Both the combined-strategy instruction and contrastive learning raised accuracy over control; effects held at 1-week delay; did not interact with each other or with test-case novelty.
limits: Abstract only; ECG task with students, not clinicians; exact effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Support for running two routes (fast recognition plus deliberate check) and comparing, rather than only one.

source: Kulatunga-Moruzi, Brooks, Norman (2001) Coordination of analytic and similarity-based processing
finding: Both feature-based (analytic) and example-similarity processing operate in diagnosis, and their balance depends on expertise and instruction.
numbers: 12 preclinical students in dermatology: they gained by using similarity to past cases, especially for atypical cases; residents (earlier work) gained by analytic strategy.
limits: Abstract only; N=12.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis testing and retrieval of similar cases are separate routes. Retrieval of past solved cases may add to S3.

source: Norman et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning
finding: Telling doctors to be slow and thorough did not raise accuracy over telling them to be fast.
numbers: Second-year residents, 96 in 2010 (speed) and 108 in 2011 (reflect), 20 internal medicine cases. Accuracy 44.5% vs 45.0% (n.s.). Time 69 s vs 89 s per case (p<0.001). Wrong cases took 17 s longer. Accuracy correlated with licensing exam scores.
limits: Cohorts were different years, not randomised in one sitting; abstract only; computer cases without data search.
agent_relevance: Do not trigger doubt by a blanket think-carefully instruction (matches G1). Knowledge, not mode, limits accuracy.

source: Norman et al. (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
finding: Review: errors arise from both fast and slow thinking; inducing availability bias in the lab is easy, but its role in real errors is not well shown; bias-awareness teaching does not cut errors; knowledge reorganisation gives small but consistent gains.
numbers: No pooled effect size in abstract; conclusion text: bias-recognition education ineffective, knowledge-reorganisation strategies small but consistent benefits.
limits: Abstract only; narrative, not systematic, review.
agent_relevance: Core of the dropped-in-the-1980s finding: content knowledge, not process. Gain in the agent should come from better knowledge access, not more hypothesis steps.

source: Norman (2005) Research in clinical reasoning: past history and current trends
finding: Over 30 years of research gave little evidence that reasoning can be characterised in terms of general process variables; expertise is multiple coordinated representations and many solved examples.
numbers: Three traditions: general process (hypothetico-deductive era), memory probes, mental representations (scripts, schemas, exemplars).
limits: Abstract only; author is a leading critic of the process view.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation that fits the replication history: content specificity beats process. Keep the process light, the knowledge rich.

source: Joseph and Patel (1990) Domain knowledge and hypothesis generation in diagnostic reasoning
finding: Experts and near-experts both generated accurate early hypotheses; the difference was in confirming or discarding alternatives, which depended on domain knowledge.
numbers: Endocrinologists (high knowledge) vs cardiologists (low knowledge) on an endocrine case, think-aloud. No significant difference in cue selection; high-knowledge group used more relations between cues, generated accurate hypotheses early and spent the rest confirming. Low-knowledge group could not discriminate and eliminate alternatives.
limits: Abstract only; small samples; one case.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation is easy; elimination needs knowledge. In the agent, S4 test and discriminating checks matter more than S3 volume.

source: Sibbald, de Bruin, van Merrienboer (2013) Checklists improve experts diagnostic decisions
finding: A checklist used at the verification step corrected more errors in expert ECG reading without raising cognitive load.
numbers: 15 experts, 18 ECGs, four conditions. Errors corrected 0.29 +/- 0.77 (checklist) vs 0.03 +/- 0.61 per ECG; net errors 0.39 +/- 1.14 vs 1.04 +/- 1.49 per ECG (p<0.01 both).
limits: Abstract only; N=15; ECG interpretation only; checklist at start risks expertise reversal.
agent_relevance: Place the check after the first hypothesis is formed (verify stage), not before. Fits S4 after S3.

source: Monteiro et al. (2015) Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough
finding: When residents were free to reconsider diagnoses, they revised few, and revision helped only slightly.
numbers: 47 residents (PGY1-3), 16 cases. Pass-1 mean 1.17, 1.35, 1.27 of 2 (n.s.). Revised at least one: 12/19 PGY1, 9/11 PGY2, 8/17 PGY3. Only 8% of diagnoses revised; mean score 1.20 to 1.22 of 2 (t=2.15, p=0.03).
limits: Self-directed reflection; no forced differential; page text read was the abstract and metadata only (PMC full text not returned).
agent_relevance: Self-chosen second looks add almost nothing. Revision should be forced by a check failure and use new data (G1, G2).

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of LLMs in clinical decision-making (Nat Med)
finding: In a realistic step-by-step setting (MIMIC-CDM, 2,400 cases, four abdominal diseases) open LLMs diagnosed worse than doctors, skipped guideline tests, and were sensitive to the order and amount of information.
numbers: Subset n=80: LLMs (20 seeds) significantly worse than 4 clinicians (P<0.001); clinicians 87.5% (German residents) and 92.5% (US hospitalist). Authors write the models show a tendency to diagnose before fully understanding a patient's case. Llama 2 Chat mean diagnostic average 45.5% in the sequential setting vs 58.8% with full information.
limits: Models are 2023-24 open-weight (Llama 2, WizardLM, OASST); does not test current reasoning models; the best order of information differs per disease.
agent_relevance: Early closure and order sensitivity are LLM failure modes the hypothesis-test loop must control in code (fixed data order, forced test of top hypotheses).

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (o1-preview)
finding: o1-preview matched or beat GPT-4 and physicians on differential generation, test choice and reasoning documentation, but gains were not uniform.
numbers: NEJM CPCs (143 cases): correct diagnosis in differential 78.3% (CI 70.7-84.8), first suggestion correct 52%. On 70 shared cases: exact or very close 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9% (p=.015). Right test chosen 87.5%. R-IDEA perfect score 78/80 vs GPT-4 47/80, attendings 28/80, residents 16/80. Landmark cases: o1 97% vs GPT-4 92%, physicians 74-76%, differences vs physicians not significant (p=0.055 to 0.076).
limits: Controls are historical in places; possible contamination (no difference before vs after cutoff: 79.8% vs 73.5%, p=0.59); text-only cases; authors stress need for prospective trials.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models cover the hypothesis list well without a scaffold; scaffold value must be shown against such models at equal tokens.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
finding: Reasoning-enhanced variants scored higher on 1,273 clinical vignettes but were not consistently less vulnerable to cognitive-bias prompts; debiasing instructions and few-shot examples did cut biased answers.
numbers: Correct rates, reasoning vs base: Llama-3.3-70B 72.5-82.1% vs 61.0-73.4%; Qwen3-32B 71.7-78.7% vs 55.5-64.1%; Gemini-2.5-Flash 81.8-88.6% vs 80.0-83.7%. Gemini on four unpublished bias prompts fell from 80.0-88.6% to 47.4-86.1%. Reasoning amplified some biases in Llama and Gemini.
limits: Single-turn multiple choice; contamination suspected for published bias prompts; three model families.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on a stated hypothesis is a real LLM risk. Prompt-level debiasing works; reasoning mode alone does not. Never feed the agent a suggested diagnosis (G5).

source: Croskerry (2013) Cognitive debiasing 1: origins of bias and theory of debiasing
finding: Theory paper: debiasing works by decoupling from the intuitive answer and deliberately engaging analytic checking, but needs awareness that a bias may be at play.
numbers: No quantified effect sizes. Authors pose the open questions: can debiasing repair biased judgments, and can environment be changed to lower bias.
limits: Opinion/theory; no data; its premise conflicts with Norman 2017, who finds bias-awareness teaching ineffective.
agent_relevance: Trigger rule for checking (a signal, not a schedule) is consistent with G1; the human evidence for training is weak.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Effects of interacting with an LLM compared with a human coach: study protocol (BMJ Open)
finding: Registered design to test whether training on widening the hypothesis space changes number of hypotheses, information search, accuracy and confidence in fourth-year medical students using ChatGPT or a human coach.
numbers: Protocol only; no results in this document. Predicts that training with a rationale for expanding the hypothesis space will raise number and relevance of hypotheses and final accuracy.
limits: No data; prediction not a finding. Check for the results paper before citing.
agent_relevance: Direct test of whether more hypotheses help in an LLM-assisted setting; watch for the result.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Nat Med: order and quantity of information
finding: LLM diagnosis changed with the order in which case data were given, and the best order differed by disease; adding relevant information sometimes lowered accuracy.
numbers: Pancreatitis diagnosis improved by 21 points or more for some models when only radiologist reports were given; some orders hurt diverticulitis (about -4 points for one model). Exact per-model tables not read.
limits: Open-weight models of 2023-24; effects are model and disease specific; numbers partly read from running text.
agent_relevance: Human case-based reasoning shows anchoring from early data too. Fix data order in code and test a hypothesis against data given in more than one order (G3, mutated input).
